items.stem: Who sings this ode?
options: The elders of Colonus
Antigone by herself
Oedipus to the king
Theseus from the altar

items.stem: To what is Oedipus compared?
options: A headland battered by storms from every side
A tree swept away in a sudden winter flood
A hunted bull running through the sacred grove
A ship already safe inside the quiet harbour

items.stem: Complete the line: “E’en as some _____ on an iron-bound shore,”
options: harbour
meadow
temple
headland

items.stem: Complete the line: “_____ by the wintry blasts and surge’s roar,”
options: Warmed
Sheltered
Praised
Lashed

items.stem: What stage of life does the ode call the worst?
options: Unregarded age
Childhood in the house
Youth with its giddy train
The hour of a marriage bell

items.stem: Which troubles does the ode list?
options: Envy, sedition, strife, carnage and war
Feasts, dances, and easy rewards of fame
Wealth, honour, and a quiet old age
Love, friendship, and the care of children

items.stem: From which directions do the winds strike the imagined headland?
options: From every side: sunset, morning, noon, and the north
From the harbour of Athens only, in a single gust
From Thebes alone, as a sign the guest must return
From underground, as if the shore itself were sinking

items.stem: In what mood do the elders of Colonus sing this ode?
options: In grief, as aged men lamenting a long and burdened life
In triumph, celebrating a Theban victory already won
In comic relief after the curse upon the sons
In a festive wedding hymn for the daughters

items.stem: What does the chorus call the man who craves excess of days?
options: A giddy wight who walks in folly's ways
A hero already sure of a quiet and easy end
A king who has earned a still longer life here
A boy who has not yet learned to hope at all

items.stem: Complete the line: “He too our _____ hath known,”
options: host
guest
king
foe

items.stem: Complete the line: “By drear misfortune’s _____ tide,”
options: whelming
gentle
distant
sudden

items.stem: Why is a headland a fitting image for the guest in this ode?
options: He stands fixed and is beaten from every side, not sunk
He is pictured as sailing safely out of Attica before night comes
He is pictured as already buried on a hidden northern shore
He is pictured as leading the whole chorus back home to Thebes

items.stem: Who, besides the singers, has known the ills the ode describes?
options: Oedipus, the man the singers include with themselves
Theseus, whom they name as a fellow singer of the ode
Creon, whom they name as a welcome friend in the grove
Polyneices, whom they name as already gone from the land

items.stem: What happens, in the ode's account, when youth has passed?
options: Troubles and toils follow, and none escapes life's coils
A quiet harbour opens and every last pain is lifted
The guest is told to return at once toward Thebes
The chorus breaks off and refuses to name any of the pain

items.stem: What judgment does the chorus pass on the man who wants more than a common span of life?
options: It judges that craving as giddy folly, scorning a common span
It praises him as the wisest and kindest guest in all Attica
It names him already sure of an honoured, quiet, famous grave
It asks Theseus to grant him twice the whole span of years

items.stem: Complete the line: “By every wind of heaven _____”
options: uplifted
forgotten
sheltered
o’erborne

items.stem: Complete the line: “Some from the sunset, some from _____ morn,”
options: western
southern
northern
orient

items.stem: Why compare Oedipus to a headland rather than to a ship?
options: A headland stands fixed and is beaten, but is not pictured as sunk
A headland can raise its anchor and leave the rocky shore at will
A ship would hide the guest's true name from every beating wind
A ship would mean the daughters had already sailed for home at once

items.stem: What does the claim that these ills are 'not I alone' add to the ode?
options: The elders include themselves, then turn those ills toward their guest
The elders deny that Oedipus has suffered any hardship at all in this song
The elders announce that the son has already been cursed in this very hour
The elders ask to keep the resting-place hidden from every later visitor

items.stem: In the ode's sequence, what makes unregarded age the worst stage?
options: It is called joyless, companionless and slow, the crowning woe
It is called the only stage that still increases every lasting joy
It is called a return of childhood, free of every heavy burden
It is called the hour when the guest is sent back toward Thebes

items.stem: Complete the line: “Some from the _____ glow.”
options: noonday
twilight
midnight
winter

items.stem: Complete the line: “Some from _____ gloom of everlasting snow.”
options: Athenian
Theban
Argive
Rhipean

items.stem: What is the effect of naming winds from sunset, morning, noon, and Rhipean snow?
options: The blows seem to come from every quarter of the sky at once
The weather is limited to a single mild breeze from the west
The image proves that the guest has already left the shore
The directions tell the daughters to sail home before night

items.stem: How should the line that names Death as a deliverer be understood in this ode?
options: As personification inside a lament by aged singers
As a stage direction telling the guest to leave the grove at once
As a promise that Oedipus has already been taken from the sacred grove
As a joke meant to cancel the rest of the song

items.stem: What does the chorus mean by saying that none escapes life's coils?
options: After youth, the ode sees troubles tightening around every life it names
The guest has already slipped the coils and left the land for good now
Only the sons of Oedipus are said to escape every last kind of pain
The coils are a legal bond Theseus can unfasten at will this very hour

items.stem: What is the effect of calling the last stage 'unregarded age'?
options: It pictures that last stage as ignored and joyless, the crowning woe in the song
It pictures that last stage as the one crowds come to honour and to praise
It pictures that last stage as a quiet prize already claimed in full by him
It pictures that last stage as a return to Thebes under a son's close protection
